newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Indonesia asks church burning to be hushed up.
newsitem.headline: Indonesia asks church burning to be hushed up.

text.p: The governor of the Indonesian province where thousands rioted last week, burning 10 churches and killing five people, has called for the attacks to be hushed up, the official Antara news agency said on Sunday.

East Java Governor Basofi Sudirman, flanked by the province's military and police chiefs, told a news conference in Malang on Saturday that the incident in the town of Situbondo on Thursday came under the government's acronym SARA relating to sensitive issues of race, religion and ethnicity.
"The incident involving the mass disturbance of the crowd in Situbondo on October 10 was purely a SARA incident," he said.
"Let us have the same aim when reporting it. This does not mean we will hide the facts, but this issue is very complex. Let us agree to hush up the problem," he said.
Antara said local security authorities were questioning 40 suspects after the incident. Officials said on Friday that at least 120 had been initially detained.

Sudirman said a crowd of between 2,000 and 3,000 people, angry with the proceedings against a man being tried on blasphemy charges, went on the rampage destroying places of worship, offices, schools and shops.
Security forces quickly regained control, he said, adding the situation had returned to normal.
Police said nine churches in Situbondo, four Christian schools, a convent and the court house were damaged. Other sources said a church in a neighbouring town and six schools were destroyed.
The accused, a Moslem, had angered the people by saying a well-known local preacher had died in an unnatural way and the prophet Mohammad was not a envoy of God for all mankind.
"In the trial, the prosecutor demanded a sentence of five years jail because the slander had been proven but the crowd was not satisfied. They demanded the death sentence," Sudirman said.
"The prosecutor himself explained that a five year sentence was already the maximum," he said.
Police said the reason why the crowd attacked churches was not clear. One report said the crowd was told the accused was hiding from them in a church adjacent to the court house.
On June 9, in the East Java capital of Surabaya 10 churches were attacked and burnt by Moslem crowds during Sunday services. The incidents were not reported in local media.

Similarily, an attack on September 17 on a building used as a church in East Jakarta was also suppressed. Police at the scene seized all the film from the cameras of parishioners and journalists who visited the site in a the semi-rural Bekasi area.
Indonesia is the world's largest Moslem nation with around 85 percent of its more than 195 million people following Islam.
